name: Dummy Deck
description: Sandbox for testing new technical phrases before migration.

cards.sideA: Necesitamos ese ambiente clonado para reproducir el problema.

sideB.text: We need that environment cloned to reproduce the problem.
We need that environment cloned so we can reproduce the issue.
We need a clone of that environment to reproduce the problem.
We need that cloned environment to reproduce the problem.

cards.sideA: Vuelvo en un minuto.

sideB.text: I'll be back in a minute.
Back in a minute.
I'll be right back.
I'll be right back in a minute.
I'll come back in a minute.

cards.note: ~I'll come in a minute~ means you will arrive at a place, but it does not imply returning ([volver]). To express returning, use [come back] or [be back].

cards.sideA: Ya regreso.

sideB.text: I'm coming right back.
I'll be back shortly.
Be right back.
I'm coming back.
I'll be back soon.
I'll be right back.
I'll be back.
I'll come back.

cards.note: ~I'll come~ means you are going to arrive, not that you are returning. Use [be back] or [come back] to express "regreso".

cards.sideA: Sí, estoy acá, solo que el audio se sobrepone con ambos micrófonos abiertos.

sideB.text: Yes, I'm here, it's just that the audio overlaps when both microphones are open.
Yes, I'm here, the audio just overlaps with both mics open.
Yes, I'm here, it's just that having both microphones open makes the audio overlap.
Yes, I'm here, it's just that the audio gets overlapped when both microphones are open.
Yes, I'm here, it's just that the audio overlaps when both microphones are opened.

cards.note: Yes, [open] can function as both an adjective and a verb. In this context, it acts as an adjective describing the state of the microphones.

cards.sideA: El audio se sobrepone al tener los 2 micrófonos abiertos.

sideB.text: The audio overlaps when both microphones are open.
The audio overlaps when you have both mics on.
Having both microphones open causes the audio to overlap.
The audio overlaps when 2 microphones are open.
The audio gets overlapped when both microphones are open.

cards.note: ~The audio gets overlapped having both microphones open~ sounds unnatural because the clause [having both microphones open] needs a connector. It is better to say [when having] or use a subordinate clause like [when both microphones are open].

cards.sideA: Se supone que este arreglada eso.

sideB.text: That's supposed to be fixed.
That's supposed to already be fixed.
That issue is supposed to be fixed already.

cards.note: ~It's supposed to be fixed that~ is incorrect because you cannot use both [It] and [that] as subjects/objects in this way. You can say [That is supposed to be fixed] or [It is supposed to be fixed].

cards.sideA: Ahora mismo no puedo emular la aplicacion, estoy de manos atadas.

sideB.text: Right now I can't emulate the application, my hands are tied.
I can't emulate the app right now, my hands are tied.
Right now I can't run the emulator for the app; there's nothing I can do.

cards.note:
~Right now I can't emulate the application, I'm hands tied~ is incorrect. The correct idiom is [my hands are tied], not "I'm hands tied".

~...I have both hands tied~ is not used for the figurative idiom. The fixed expression is [my hands are tied].

cards.sideA: Ahora mismo estoy de manos atadas, no puedo testearlo.

sideB.text: Right now my hands are tied, I can't test it.
My hands are tied right now, so I can't test it.
I can't test it right now, there's nothing I can do.

cards.note:
~Right now I'm hands tied, I can't test it~ is incorrect because the expression is [my hands are tied]. You cannot say "I'm hands tied".

~Right now I have both hands tied, I can't test it~ is incorrect for the idiom. While grammatically fine for a literal situation, the figurative expression is always [my hands are tied].

cards.sideA: Toca cada tarjeta de marca aquí.

sideB.text: Tap each brand tile here.
Tap on each brand tile here.
Tap each brand card here.

cards.note:
In UI design, a [tile] is usually a flat, clickable square or rectangle that navigates to a new section or launches an app, whereas a [card] often contains more complex, heterogeneous information (text, images, buttons) grouped together.

~Touch each brand tile here~ is understandable, but for digital interfaces and screens, the correct verb is [tap]. [Touch] is generally used for physical contact rather than interacting with a UI element.

cards.sideA: Los bloques de marca mejoraron las ventas.

sideB.text: Brand tiles improved sales.
Brand tiles boosted sales.
The brand tiles improved sales performance.
Brand tiles improved the sales.

cards.sideA: La conversacion se perdio para siempre, o solo temporalmente?

sideB.text: Is the conversation lost forever, or only temporarily?
Is the conversation lost for good, or only temporarily?
Is the conversation gone forever, or just for now?

cards.note:
**[er:12]**

~Does the conversation lose forever...~ and ~Did the conversation lose forever...~ are incorrect because [lose] is active. A conversation cannot lose something; it must be passive ([is the conversation lost] or [did the conversation get lost]).

cards.sideA: Cuando A es diferente de B, podemos acceder.

sideB.text: When A is different from B, we can access it.
When A differs from B, we can gain access.
We can access it when A is different from B.
When A is different to B, we can access it.

cards.note: ~When A is different from B, we can access~ is missing an object. The verb [access] is transitive in English and requires a direct object (e.g., [access it], [gain access]).

cards.sideA: Las devoluciones usan bandejas.

sideB.text: Returns use flats.
Returns are processed using flats.
Flats are used for returns.
Returns use trays.

cards.note: In logistics and mail sorting, a [flat] refers to a large envelope, magazine, or a flat sorting tray. A [tray] is a shallow container used to hold, sort, or carry items.

cards.sideA: No está sobreescribiendo lo que nos llega del backend, no hay problema.

sideB.text: It's not overwriting what we get from the backend, so there's no problem.
It isn't overwriting what comes in from the backend, no issue there.
There's no problem, it's not overwriting the data coming from the backend.
It's not overwriting what we received from the backend, so there's no problem.
It isn't overwriting what comes from the backend, so there is no issue there.

cards.sideA: Con respecto a su propuesta, necesitamos más tiempo para revisar los detalles.

sideB.text: Regarding your proposal, we need more time to review the details.
With respect to your proposal, we need more time to go over the details.
Regarding your proposal, we need some extra time to review the details.

cards.sideA: A pesar del clima, el evento al aire libre se llevará a cabo según lo programado.

sideB.text: Regardless of the weather, the outdoor event will proceed as scheduled.
Despite the weather, the outdoor event will go ahead as planned.
Regardless of the weather, the outdoor event will take place as scheduled.

cards.note:
**[er:33]**

~Regardless the weather...~ is incorrect because the preposition [of] is missing. The correct fixed phrase is [regardless of].

cards.sideA: La rama local esta adelantada a la rama remota.

sideB.text: The local branch is ahead of the remote branch.
The local branch is ahead of the remote one.
The local branch has commits the remote branch doesn't.

cards.note: ~The local branch is ahead from the remote branch~ is incorrect because the preposition used with 'ahead' is [of], not 'from'.

cards.sideA: La rama local esta detras de la rama remota.

sideB.text: The local branch is behind the remote branch.
The local branch is behind the remote one.
The local branch is lagging behind the remote branch.

cards.note: ~The local branch is behind from/of/to the remote branch~ are all incorrect. The word [behind] acts directly as the preposition here, so it doesn't need 'from', 'of', or 'to'. It is simply [behind the remote branch].

cards.sideA: Solo espero que no se corte la luz.

sideB.text: I just hope the power doesn't go out.
I just hope we don't lose power.
I only hope the electricity doesn't go out.
I just hope the power doesn't cut off.
I just hope the power doesn't cut out.
I just hope the power doesn't go off.

cards.sideA: Podría tomar un tiempo, debo mirar primero el código de la BD y luego el código Mobile.

sideB.text: It could take a while. I need to look at the database code first and then the mobile code.
This might take some time. I have to check the database code first and then the mobile code.
It may take a while. First I need to review the database code, then the mobile code.

cards.sideA: Podría tomar cerca de 1 hora. Debo mirar si el código mobile sobreescribe lo que recibimos de la BD.

sideB.text: It could take about an hour. I need to check whether the mobile code overwrites what we get from the database.
This might take around one hour. I have to see if the mobile code is overriding what we receive from the database.
It may take close to an hour. I need to look at whether the mobile code overwrites the data we get from the database.
It could take around an hour. I need to check if the mobile code overwrites what we get from the database.

cards.note: ~I need to check if the mobile code overwriten what we get from the database.~ is not valid because [overwriten] is not an existing form. The verb goes [overwrite] → [overwrote] → [overwritten], and the participle only works with an auxiliary ([has overwritten], [is overwritten]). After 'if the mobile code', the present simple [overwrites] is the form that fits.

cards.sideA: Quiero la mitad del pastel.

sideB.text: I want half of the cake.
I want half the cake.
I would like half of the cake.

cards.note:
**[er:229]**

~I want the half of the cake.~ is not valid because [half] does not take 'the' in front of it in this structure. The natural forms are [half the cake] and [half of the cake], and with an article it becomes [a half].

cards.sideA: Quiero la cuarta parte del pastel.

sideB.text: I want a quarter of the cake.
I want one fourth of the cake.
I would like a quarter of the cake.
I want a fourth of the cake.

cards.sideA: No está bien, pero es aceptable. ¿Es aceptable?

sideB.text: It's not fine, but it's acceptable. Is it acceptable?
It's not great, but it's acceptable. Is that acceptable?
It's not right, but it's good enough. Is it acceptable?

cards.sideA: Desde dónde estamos obteniendo la información está muy lento.

sideB.text: Where we are getting the information from is very slow.
The place we are getting the information from is very slow.
The source we are pulling the information from is very slow.

cards.note:
**[er:230]**

~From we are getting the information is very slow.~ is not valid because a clause cannot begin with the bare preposition in this pattern. The clause starts with the wh-word and [from] stays at the end: [where we are getting the information from].

cards.sideA: Hablemos de esto fuera de línea.

sideB.text: Let's take this offline.
Let's take it offline.
Let's discuss this offline.

cards.note: ~Let's keep this offline.~ changes the meaning: it suggests not publishing something online or keeping it off the record. To move a discussion out of the current meeting and handle it separately, the fixed expression is [take this offline] or [discuss this offline].

cards.sideA: No construyas las vistas que quedan aún.

sideB.text: Don't build the remaining views yet.
Do not build the views that are still left.
Don't build the views that are left yet.

cards.sideA: Todavía es un trabajo en progreso.

sideB.text: It's still a work in progress.
It is still work in progress.
That's still a work in progress.

cards.sideA: Tan pronto como Red se levante, actualizaré la contraseña del usuario.

sideB.text: As soon as Red is up, I will update the user's password.
As soon as Red comes up, I'll update the user's password.
As soon as Red is back up, I will update the user's password.

cards.sideA: Le mantendremos informado sobre nuestro progreso.

sideB.text: We'll keep you posted on our progress.
We will keep you updated on our progress.
We'll keep you posted with our progress.
We'll keep you informed about our progress.

cards.note: ~We'll keep you inform about our progress.~ is not valid because [inform] is the base verb and cannot describe the state of a person. After [keep + object] the word must be an adjective or a participle, so the correct form is [keep you informed], the same pattern as [keep you posted] and [keep you updated].

cards.sideA: Sí, pero siempre bajo la dirección de Juan.

sideB.text: Yes, but always under Juan's direction.
Yes, but always under Juan's guidance.
Yes, but always led by Juan.

cards.sideA: En problemas difíciles suele ser Jose quien me dice cuál puede ser el problema, y posibles soluciones.

sideB.text: With hard problems, it's usually Jose who tells me what the problem might be, and possible solutions.
On difficult problems, it's usually Jose who tells me what the issue could be and possible solutions.
For tough problems, it's normally Jose who tells me what the problem might be and what the possible solutions are.

cards.note:
~it's used to be Jose~ is not valid because [used to] never combines with the present of 'to be'. For a present habit the word is [usually] or [normally]; [it used to be Jose] exists but moves the sentence to a past habit that is no longer true.

~In hard problems~ is not natural because English does not place problems inside a container here. The usual collocations are [with hard problems], [on difficult problems] or [for tough problems].

cards.sideA: Sí, pero siempre con la supervisión de Roberto.

sideB.text: Yes, but always with Roberto's supervision.
Yes, but always under Roberto's supervision.
Yes, but always with oversight from Roberto.
